newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin opens crusade to save reforms from crime.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin opens crusade to save reforms from crime.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, in the first major policy statement of his second term, will launch an anti-corruption drive to restore order to the Russian economy and stop graft and crime from strangling market reforms.

In Thursday's annual state of the nation address to parliament, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, Yeltsin said: "Most Russians are unhappy with today and scared of tomorrow...The people's patience has run out."
"The difficult economic situation and disastrous situation in the social sector demand concerted, energetic action."

Giving no details of the government shake-up that is expected to follow his speech, he said criminal "godfathers" were openly challenging the state with the connivance of corrupt officials and threatening democratic market reforms begun after Soviet communism collapsed in 1991.

"When free buying and selling extends to the passing of laws, to the work of civil servants and to court decisions, it is not just immoral but a mortal danger to society and the state," Yeltsin said in an address short on specific measures.

Kremlin sources said he is likely to name liberal economist Anatoly Chubais, currently his chief-of-staff, to a powerful new government post under Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin with sweeping powers to implement a clean-up campaign.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky, in comments to Interfax news agency, denied reports that Chubais had already been appointed first deputy prime minister.
Chubais, 41, is popular with foreign investors but hated by the communists who dominate parliament and who accuse him of corruption in his management of Russia's privatisation drive.
The St. Petersburg economist has a reputation as an outstanding administrator, which could allow the convalescent Yeltsin to play a more hands-off role.

His speech at 11 a.m. (0800 GMT) will be based on, but not identical to, the written address. Kremlin sources said it will last half an hour -- 10 minutes less than suggested earlier. It is a big test of the 66-year-old leader's health after spending the first eight months of his second term out of action.
Yeltsin has not appeared for so long in public since a strenuous campaign for last July's presidential election which left him needing bypass surgery to correct a heart problem.

"It will test his strength and ability to rule," said Andrei Piontkowski, head of the independent Centre for Strategic Studies. "He has been getting more and more confident and it looks like everything is okay now."
Yeltsin has looked increasingly well as he gradually stepped up his visits to the Kremlin following the pneumonia in January which stalled his political comeback.

Thursday's speech in the Kremlin's Marble Hall, the former home of Communist Party meetings, will be a summary of the long-written document called a poslaniye (message) which sets out policy for the year ahead and will be handed out to legislators.
On foreign policy, Yeltsin indicated he would press on with plans for closer integration with former Soviet states, notably Belarus.
Proposals to unite with this western neighbour could be a response to NATO's planned eastward expansion. Yeltsin warned Europe it needed to work with Russia if it wanted security.

After publicly scolding ministers and other top officials in recent days, Yeltsin made no specific attacks on the conduct of the government in his address, although he repeated his demand that deeply unpopular backlogs in the payment of wages and pensions must be cleared.

Having criticised Defence Minister Igor Rodionov last week for "whinging" over the difficulties of army reform, Yeltsin appeared to backtrack on his election campaign pledge to end conscription by the end of the century. He said a structural overhaul was needed before Russia had a fully professional army.
